stances.claim: The SC docket is being clogged by an unusual surge of 'transcendental' constitutionality cases — Comelec GAD, VP Sara Duterte impeachment, GAA, PhilHealth, MIF — all requiring en banc treatment and time-consuming oral arguments, deserving public sympathy ('pity the Supreme Court justices').

Sovereign wealth funds are not uncommon globally — Norway's $222.4B 2024 profit (largest in the world), Singapore's GIC and Temasek, Indonesia's just-launched Danantara — so the MIF concept itself is not the constitutional infirmity; the question is the manner of enactment.

Whether the Court will revise the Enrolled Bill Doctrine remains to be seen at the April 22 oral argument.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with institutional empathy: 'Pity the Supreme Court justices. Their clogged dockets are being crowded further by numerous new transcendental cases' -- most involving constitutionality issues elevated to the banc and invariably requiring time-consuming oral arguments, including Comelec gravely-abusive acts, VP Sara Duterte's impeachment, the GAA, PhilHealth (last Monday's column), and the Maharlika Investment Fund (MIF) case filed by Sen. Koko Pimentel and Bayan Muna. He notes his deliberate restraint ('I will not risk contempt of court by commenting on the merits of the case. I will write only to enable the public to understand the vital issues at stake') and provides global context: sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) are not uncommon -- Norway's, the largest in the world, posted a full-year 2024 profit of $222.4 billion (2.5 trillion kroner) at 13% ROI, set up in the 1990s from oil-and-gas excess revenues, investing in 8,000+ companies in 63 countries; Singapore has GIC and Temasek; Indonesia just launched Danantara on Feb 24 under President Prabowo Subianto, modeled on Temasek with about $20 billion planned for science, technology, and AI. The petitioners challenge Republic Act No. 11954 as void for violating Section 26(2) of Article VI and Sections 16 and 20 of Article XII; among several arguments, the most essential is the alleged violation of Section 26(2)'s requirements that a bill must pass 'three readings on separate days, and printed copies thereof in its final form have been distributed to its members three days before its passage' (except on presidential certification for public calamity or emergency), with no amendment on the last reading and the yeas and nays entered in the Journal. The OSG, led by 'the esteemed Menardo I. Guevarra,' counters with the Enrolled Bill Doctrine -- anchored in separation of powers, the doctrine holds that the bill certified by the Senate President, Senate Secretary, House Speaker, and House Secretary, and signed or lapsed into law by the President, conclusively binds the judiciary, notwithstanding extrinsic evidence (media reports, member interviews, member speeches). The same doctrine is the government's main defense in parallel transcendental cases involving the GAA and other laws. Panganiban notes the reciprocity: the same separation-of-powers logic bars congressional or executive inquiry into the SC's internal deliberations, with signatures on the file copy at the Office of the Clerk of Court deemed the true and authentic decision regardless of personal declarations of incumbent or retired justices (including his own). But 'nothing is really written in stone in law and jurisprudence. It is said that the law must be stable, but it cannot stand still' -- the SC has reversed even his own rulings (the marginalized-and-underrepresented restriction on the party-list system, and the directory-only reading of the 20% party-list share, both later overturned). Whether the present Court will revise or modify the Enrolled Bill Doctrine, the April 22 oral argument may give a hint. Abangan.
